question: Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1217, which was motivated by isolated outbreaks of sheep pox, places a total ban on movements and exports of live sheep from Romania to the single market. Although protecting animal health is a legitimate aim, this measure is contrary to the principle of proportionality. In similar crises within the EU, the Commission has applied surgical regionalisation, isolating the affected areas.

The collective penalisation of the whole of Romania is distorting competition, leaving production at a standstill and directly favouring competitors in the rest of the EU. The ban on transportation by land is forcing Romanians to bear asymmetrical logistical costs for third markets, pushing family farms towards bankruptcy.

This artificial collapse in producer prices is solely benefiting large industrial slaughterhouses, which are imposing monopoly prices. At the same time, the elimination of the biggest exporter of live sheep will cause an inflationary shock in the consumer markets of importing Member States. 1.
What technical justifications underlie the refusal to apply the principle of strict regionalisation for Romania, by contrast with the procedures applied in western countries?
How does the Commission plan to mitigate the market abuse perpetrated by large processors against Romanian farmers, who are being forced to sell at prices below their production costs?
Will the Commission activate mechanisms of direct compensation from the agricultural crisis reserve to prevent this strategic sector from going bankrupt?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.8.2026) At EU level, Regulation (EU) 2016/4291 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/6872 regulate sheep pox and goat pox.

In Romania, Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/11083 introduced additional temporary emergency measures including a restriction on the movement of sheep and goats from the entire territory of Romania to other Member States or third countries, considering that the disease situation is uncertain and deteriorating.

Preliminary surveillance results in May-June 2026 identified seropositive establishments outside the currently existing restricted zones, indicating possible wider circulation of the disease. The Commission works with Romania on further eradication measures, including emergency vaccination. The EU has introduced several tools to strengthen the farmers position in the food chain.

Regulation (EU) No 1308/20134 reinforces written contracts, cost-based price formulas and mediation. Directive (EU) 2019/6335 on unfair trading practices is being revised, to address cases where farmers are forced to systematically sell below production costs, while maintaining the Common Agricultural Policy market orientation.

The Commission may adopt exceptional support measures for market losses due to restrictions imposed for disease control. Under Regulation (EU) 2021/21156, countries may amend their CAP Strategic Plans to provide crisis payment and support investments to restore agricultural production after animal disease outbreaks, and grant aid in line with EU State aid rules.
